provider: World Bank Open Data (Indicators API v2)

free_tier.stated: 'API keys and other authentication methods are no longer necessary to access the API.' Nearly 16,000 time series indicators across over 45 databases, many series back over 50 years.
free_tier.notes: No rate limit is published anywhere on the API documentation.

per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: JSON or XML per call, with per_page up to 32,000 rows on some indicators. The responses measured here were 9,735-13,760 bytes each at per_page=50.

retention.stated: the indicator series are revised in place; there is no versioned snapshot endpoint documented

egress.terms: Free and unmetered. No key, no account, no attribution gate at the transport level.

tooling: curl/python-requests; wbgapi and pandas-datareader wrap it. No SDK needed.
chaining: The economic and social join keys for any national-level dataset; it is metadata-density, not byte-volume, so it pairs with a large byte source rather than replacing one.

limits.value: none published; measured 24 requests in 2.061 s at 8 connections (about 18 requests/second over the request phase) with no 429, and 20 requests in 43.774 s sequentially (latency-bound at about 2.2 s per call)

binding_note: The API returns about 11 KB per call, so 1 TiB would take roughly 95 million calls; per-call latency, not any byte quota, is what limits a day. Parallel calls help here, unlike on the file hosts.

identity_cost.detail: No key: 'API keys and other authentication methods are no longer necessary'. Anonymous GET returned 200 and 324 bytes for per_page=1.

reliability_note: Sequential calls cost about 2.2 s each from this machine, so an unparallelised harvest spends its day in latency; the API answered all 44 calls made here without a single 429.
confidence_note: 44 calls were made and counted, at 1 and 8 connections, with bytes per response recorded. What is not measured is the point at which throttling starts, because none was reached.

evidence.proved: 'API keys and other authentication methods are no longer necessary to access the API' and 'nearly 16,000 time series indicators'
20 sequential requests in 43,774 ms, 19x200 and 1 transport error, mean 10,615.8 bytes per response; sha256 of the first response a9dc0be3cba1c4bff059bfe695824288b4b542ddf13bb529ee2582bf5bcdadc3
24 requests in 2,061 ms wall, all 200, 9,735-13,760 bytes per response - no 429 at about 18 requests/second

notes: A useful contrast: on the file hosts, more connections made things slower; here eight connections made the same 24 calls 21 times faster than one. The difference is latency-bound JSON versus bandwidth-bound files.
